19 
A. 
In my current role, I provide advisory services across MISO business areas and manage 
20 
relationships with key MISO stakeholders across the central region of the MISO footprint.  
21 
Given my length and breadth of experience, I was chosen to act as the MISO liaison to the

newly-formed Large Load Working Group (“LLWG”) in March 2026.  As the LLWG

liaison, I coordinate MISO’s planned activities with respect to our large load stakeholder

efforts.  Since October 2025, I have also led MISO’s effort to create and formalize the

A. 
No. This is the first testimony that I have provided in any regulatory proceeding. 
8 
II. 
PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY 
9 
Q. 
WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY? 
10 
A. 
My testimony supports two related items.  First, my testimony supports the proposed Tariff 
11 
revisions submitted in this docket to implement Zero Injection Generator Interconnection 
12 
Service (“ZG Interconnection Service”) and a Zero Injection Generator Interconnection 
13 
Agreement (“ZGIA”) to govern and memorialize the terms of this service.  Second, my 
14 
testimony also explains how the ZGIA addresses certain findings and directives in the 
15 
Commission’s Show Cause Order related to large load integration issued to MISO in 
16 
Docket No. EL26-70-000 on June 18, 2026 (“Show Cause Order”).  This includes, but is 
17 
not limited to, how the ZGIA process aims to provide Speed to Power by increasing the 
18 
pace of generating capacity additions in the MISO region and to provide a mechanism to 
19 
better evaluate the reliability impacts of co-location and similar arrangements.  In providing 
20 
this testimony, capitalized terms not otherwise defined herein have the meeting set forth in 
21 
MISO’s Tariff.  
22 
Q. 
WHY IS THE ZGIA CONSTRUCT NEEDED? 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 3 
 
 
A. 
ZGIA implementation is needed to: (1) provide MISO with visibility into generating 
1 
resources that plan to connect to the Transmission System but not inject onto the 
2 
Transmission System; and (2) the ZGIA will allow MISO to establish a framework to 
3 
provide the necessary studies to ensure reliability of the Transmission System, without 
4 
subjecting generators that are not expected to have significant system impacts to the more 
5 
protracted interconnection queue.  The ZGIA construct also provides a benefit to the 
6 
interconnection queue, because it provides a parallel path for differently situated generators 
7 
to be studied for interconnection service.  
8 
Q. 
PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY THIS PROPOSAL IS TIME SENSITIVE. 
9 
A. 
As discussed in the Show Cause Order, the Commission has taken numerous actions in the 
10 
past year to address unprecedented increases in requests for transmission service to serve 
11 
large loads and the growing interest in the co-location of loads with generating facilities 
12 
(i.e., co-location agreements).  These actions, coupled with the Commission ANOPR 
13 
addressing the need to take additional actions related to the addition of large and co-located 
14 
loads, highlight the urgent need to implement solutions to address large load integration 
15 
and co-location arrangements in the MISO region.  
16 
 
MISO agrees that it is experiencing an unprecedented surge in large load additions, 
17 
primarily from data centers. In recognition of the urgent need to address speed to reliable 
18 
power and associated network upgrades, MISO established the Expedited Resource 
19 
Addition Study (“ERAS”) process to accelerate the generator interconnection process and 
20 
improved MTEP’s Expedited Project Review (“EPR”) process to quickly approve 
21 
transmission network upgrades needed to integrate large loads.  While existing processes 
22 
have effectively integrated new large loads, MISO needs to continue to evolve its approach 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 4 
 
 
and develop long-term solutions to maintain reliability while enabling accelerating load 
1 
growth. 
2 
This accelerating load growth poses an increasing reliability challenge to the grid, and has 
3 
been discussed, documented and highlighted in various MISO and non-MISO reports.1   
4 
Finally, large load can have different enablement needs and pose operational challenges 
5 
and opportunities that differ from traditional load additions.  This filing is urgently needed 
6 
to provide an enablement path directly responsive to the specific needs of co-located 
7 
generation and large loads.  As MISO continues to receive such requests, having a ZGIA 
8 
process available will improve the speed, efficiency, and reliability of such integrations.  
9 
III. 
THE CURRENT STATE OF THE MISO QUEUE AND THE NEED FOR ZG 
10 
INTERCONNECTION SERVICE 
11 
Q. 
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE EFFECTIVENESS OF MISO’S INTERCONNECTION 
12 
QUEUE PROCESS FOR ADDRESSING THE NEEDS OF LARGE LOADS. 
13 
A. 
MISO’s Interconnection Queue, known as the Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”), 
14 
provides a valuable tool that processes a significant volume of generation requests each 
15 
study cycle.  The DPP processes most Interconnection Requests for new Generating 
16 
Facilities and Energy storage Resources.  It will continue to be the primary tool for meeting 
17 
most load growth needs, including some large loads.  
18

However, the number of generator interconnection requests in the MISO queue continues 
1 
to be extraordinary and unprecedented. As of July 2026, MISO’s generator interconnection 
2 
queue contains 802 active Interconnection Requests comprising 167 GW of proposed new 
3 
generator interconnection capacity. This considerable volume of applications is spread 
4 
over all five of MISO’s study regions and includes queue cycles going back to 2021.  MISO 
5 
has engaged in significant reform efforts to address the speed of processing the queue.  For 
6 
example, since MISO’s last major queue reform in 2017, MISO has made numerous 
7 
improvements to its queue rules.  In 2019, MISO made a filing with the Commission to 
8 
strengthen certain milestone and site control requirements. In 2021, MISO filed 
9 
improvements to its Option to Build, harm test calculation, and provisional GIA 
10 
requirements as well as filings to classify fuel type change requests made in the DPP 
11 
process as a Material Modification and allow Interconnection Customers to request Surplus 
12 
Interconnection Service earlier in the interconnection study process.  In 2022, MISO filed 
13 
an innovative proposal to reduce the GIP timeline by offering enhanced flexibility and an 
14 
optional path for Interconnection Customers to execute GIAs in under one year.  In 2023, 
15 
during the pendency of the Order No. 2023 process, MISO further strengthened its DPP 
16 
process and worked to discourage speculative Interconnection Requests through adoption 
17 
of an Automatic Withdrawal Penalty and further refinements of its site control 
18 
requirements. In addition, MISO worked with its RTO neighbors, PJM Interconnection, 
19 
LLC (“PJM”) and Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”), to improve affected system studies 
20 
procedures and requirements that are contained in MISO’s Joint Operating Agreements.  
21 
In addition to these efforts, MISO and SPP developed and filed the Joint Targeted 
22 
Interconnection Queue Study (“JTIQ”) process, which has sped the queue up considerably 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 6 
 
 
by providing an alternative to the backlogged affected systems study process with SPP 
1 
while providing both more efficient solutions to the needs of multiple cycles of 
2 
Interconnection Customers and greater up-front cost certainty regarding potentially 
3 
significant affected systems costs.  In 2024 and 2025, MISO developed and filed an 
4 
innovative ERAS process as a temporary solution to address urgent near-term resource 
5 
adequacy and reliability concerns due to load growth, generation retirement, and delays in 
6 
the interconnection process.  Beyond these filed processes, MISO has worked to develop 
7 
internal process and software improvements, such as integrated modeling software Suite 
8 
of Unified Grid Analyses with Renewables (“SUGAR”), for Phase 1 DPP studies with 
9 
plans to integrate in Phase 2 and 3.  The SUGAR software leverages powerful circuit 
10 
simulation methods developed to study billion-transistor electronic systems. SUGAR 
11 
reduced DPP phase 1 cycle time significantly from the status quo as evidenced in the DPP 
12 
2022, 2023 and 2025 cycles.  
13 
While these reforms are producing—and will continue to produce—significant 
14 
process efficiencies and allow MISO to shorten the study time needed, it would not be 
15 
feasible or desirable to truncate the DPP to the degree needed to meet the short lead times 
16 
demanded by data centers and other large loads to meet their need by dates—some of which 
17 
seek to go online within a year—without compromising the utility for the DPP for all other 
18 
types of Interconnection Requests.  
19 
The DPP enables system reliability by studying new generation sources for 
20 
technical and operational impacts on the Transmission System and identifying and 
21 
assigning the costs for the necessary upgrades required to connect the new resources safely 
22 
and reliably.  However, in limited circumstances involving generation serving load at the 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 7 
 
 
same substation or behind the same Point of Interconnection where the proposed 
1 
configuration presents a minimal likelihood of impacting the Transmission System, a 
2 
separate, expedited study process and corresponding form of Interconnection Service is 
3 
feasible and needed to meet the frequently short lead times required by certain loads, 
4 
including large loads associated with data centers. 
5 
Q. 
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE RATIONALE FOR MISO’S PROPOSAL TO 
6 
ESTABLISH A NEW FORM OF INTERCONNECTION SERVICE. 
7 
A. 
MISO is proposing a new form of interconnection service because the existing service 
8 
types are studied in a manner that is inherently broader, because they study more significant 
9 
far reaching impacts to the Transmission System.  This type of study is unnecessarily time-
10 
consuming and expensive for Interconnection Customers who seek to serve load at the 
11 
same substation.  
 
 
12 
Some Interconnection Customers—particularly those serving large loads— seek to 
13 
install generation to meet the needs of adjacent large loads, do not require access to the 
14 
transmission system and, in fact, may never intend to inject onto the MISO Transmission 
15 
System or, if they do plan on injecting, it is only to move energy to an adjacent bay of the 
16 
same substation.  Under the current Tariff, these Interconnection Customers are required 
17 
to pursue at a minimum ERIS, which grants “as available” access to the full MISO 
18 
Transmission System.  As a result, the ERIS studies must evaluate potential impacts to the 
19 
entire MISO Transmission System.  These studies must be robust, lengthy, and often 
20 
performed on groups of Interconnection Requests because they can affect the same 
21 
constraints.  Such a study process is excessive for customers whose electrical impacts are 
22 
confined to a single substation or adjacent load.  
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 8 
 
 
It would be unnecessary and burdensome to require Interconnection Customers 
1 
who do not plan to inject onto the Transmission System to proceed through the DPP due 
2 
to their limited needs.  It is unnecessary for Interconnection Customers willing to commit 
3 
to highly limited injection because the ERIS study is configured for broad “as available” 
4 
system access and the Network Upgrades needed to allow such service would not be 
5 
required by the limited Interconnection Customer.  Requiring Interconnection Customers 
6 
participating in these limited co-location arrangements to obtain ERIS would require MISO 
7 
either to model the impacts of these units far more narrowly than other Interconnection 
8 
Customers to accurately represent their impact, or to ignore the limitations on their 
9 
injection and model them as Interconnection Requests that are not as limited as planned.  
10 
The latter approach would inflate the costs of such co-location arrangements, and the 
11 
former approach essentially adds delays to what can be a much narrower and faster study 
12 
in order to maintain consistency of timing in the study group.  Neither approach is efficient 
13 
or likely to promote the expeditious development of generation to serve adjacent large 
14 
loads.  Despite the inefficiency of the DPP with respect to differently situated large loads, 
15 
and the mismatch of existing interconnection service products for Interconnection 
16 
Customers serving a single substation or adjacent load, some form of interconnection 
17 
service is needed to: (1) address the actual impacts of limited injection and ensure the 
18 
Interconnection Customer pays for any necessary upgrades associated with these limited 
19 
impacts; (2) validate the sufficiency of the Interconnection Customer’s proposed 
20 
mechanisms to limit injection; and (3) memorialize commitments, including control 
21 
equipment and operational limitations, in a binding agreement.  MISO developed ZG 
22

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 9 
 
 
Interconnection Service and the resulting ZGIA to provide transparency through a more 
1 
targeted and efficient study process.  
2 
Q. 
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE PURPOSE OF THE ZERO INJECTION GENERATOR 
3 
INTERCONNECTION AGREEMENT. 
4 
A. 
The ZGIA construct serves a number of purposes, including: (i) providing visibility into 
5 
Transmission connected generation that does not plan to inject onto the Transmission 
6 
System; (ii) providing a needed framework to confirm lack of injection and enforce 
7 
commitments; (iii) enabling a streamlined interconnection process for projects that do not 
8 
have significant system impacts; (iv) providing a lower cost Interconnection Service that 
9 
will be highly useful to large loads; and (v) ensuring that general requirements that should 
10 
apply to all generators connected to the Transmission System are uniformly applied. 
11 
Q. 
PLEASE 
DESCRIBE 
HOW 
THE 
ZG 
INTERCONNECTION 
SERVICE 
12 
REQUIREMENTS DIFFER FROM AN INTERCONNECTION REQUEST IN THE 
13 
MISO QUEUE? 
14 
A. 
The ZG Interconnection Service requirements differ from those applicable to 
15 
Interconnection Requests in the queue in several respects.  First, the resource seeking ZG 
16 
Interconnection Service must demonstrate a documented relationship with load connected 
17 
at the same voltage side of the same substation.  This ZG Associated Load must affirm its 
18 
intention to be served by the ZG Resource.  As ZG Interconnection Service limits the ZG 
19 
Resource to serving only its designated ZG Associated Load, documenting this relationship 
20 
is necessary to prevent speculative Interconnection Requests that are not tied to actual load. 
21 
Second, the Interconnection Customer seeking ZG Interconnection Service, while not 
22 
limited in the quantity of nameplate capacity of ZG Resource they choose to build, is 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 10 
 
 
limited to requesting and being awarded Interconnection Service at a level that does not 
1 
exceed the peak demand of the ZG Associated Load.  This helps ensure that expected 
2 
production does not exceed load and therefore helps prevent injections onto the 
3 
Transmission System.  Third, the ZG Interconnection Service Study must model the ZG 
4 
Associated Load when studying the Interconnection Request and confirm that the proposed 
5 
equipment to limit injections is sufficient.  Fourth, the ZG Resource must interconnect at 
6 
the same substation and voltage level as the Point(s) of Withdrawal through which it will 
7 
serve the ZG Associated Load.  Fifth, the ZG Interconnection Study must determine that 
8 
the ZG Resource will not require Network Upgrades beyond the substation except for 
9 
system protection facilities at adjacent substations.  If all of these criteria are met, the ZG 
10 
Interconnection study process affords an accelerated study process leading to a ZGIA 
11 
within 90 days that memorializes the proposed configuration and limited injection.  
12 
Q. 
WHAT ARE THE KEY DISTINCTIONS BETWEEN THE STUDY PERFORMED 
13 
UNDER THE DPP PROCESS AND THE STUDY CONDUCTED FOR A ZGIA? 
14 
A. 
The study performed under the DPP process differs from the ZGIA study in several 
15 
important respects.  Under the DPP, Interconnection Requests are evaluated through a 
16 
three-phase, grouped study process that includes decisions points designed to identify and 
17 
remove speculative projects as more information is discovered about the impact of adding 
18 
a generating resource to the Transmission System.  Because projects all impact the 
19 
Transmission System and are studied in groups, each Interconnection Request is affected 
20 
by higher-queued and same-group projects, introducing complexity and uncertainty, 
21 
particularly when withdrawals occur.  
22

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 11 
 
 
The ZGIA study, in contrast, will be conducted on a serial, first-come, first-served basis, 
1 
rather than in groups.  The ZGIA study incorporates analyses specific to the limited-
2 
injection nature of the ZG Interconnection Service to ensure system reliability, including a 
3 
required scenario where the ZG Associated Load trips offline.  Due to the different nature 
4 
of the interconnection of ZG Resources, the ZGIA study framework is sensible because of 
5 
the minimal impacts beyond the substation and therefore can be completed on a faster 
6 
timeline, in parallel to the DPP. 
7 
Q. 
WHY IS THE AMOUNT OF SERVICE REQUESTED AND AWARDED LIMITED 
8 
TO THE PEAK DEMAND OF THE ZG ASSOCIATED LOAD AND THE 
9 
NAMEPLATE CAPACITY OF THE ZG RESOURCE IS NOT LIMITED? 
10 
A. 
The service award limitation of ZG Interconnection Service serves to ensure that the 
11 
maximum expected energy production of the ZG Resource is no greater than the maximum 
12 
demand of the ZG Associated Load, and as a result, the ZG Resource does not inject more 
13 
broadly onto the Transmission System. The additional nameplate capacity allows the ZG 
14 
Resource to achieve sufficient accredited capacity to meet the ZG Associated Load within 
15 
the MISO capacity construct, where accreditation varies by resource type.  It is also 
16 
permissible because nameplate capacity does not determine the level of Interconnection 
17 
Service.  An Interconnection Customer may not inject in excess of its Interconnection 
18 
Service level. 
19 
Q. 
WHY DOES MISO PROPOSE TO LIMIT ZG INTERCONNECTION SERVICE 
20 
TO ARRANGEMENTS WHERE THE ZG RESOURCE AND THE ZG 
21 
ASSOCIATED LOAD ARE LOCATED ON THE SAME VOLTAGE SIDE OF THE 
22 
SAME SUBSTATION? 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 12 
 
 
A. 
MISO developed this requirement after extensive stakeholder discussions and considering 
1 
various alternatives including both limiting ZG Interconnection Service to the same Point 
2 
of Interconnection or, conversely, expanding it to allow the generation and ZG Associated 
3 
Load to be separated by one or more substations.  As part of these discussions, MISO 
4 
received strong stakeholder opposition to broadening ZG Interconnection Service to 
5 
embrace what the Show Cause Order refers to as electrically proximate load.  Stakeholders, 
6 
including developers, Transmission Owners, and other entities argued that this broader 
7 
scope was more than what was needed to enable large loads and would undermine the 
8 
ability to ensure limited injection to the rest of the Transmission System.   
9 
Stakeholders, including those who have developed or plan to develop large loads 
10 
for interconnection to the MISO Transmission System, also opined that limiting ZG 
11 
Interconnection Service to a single Point of Interconnection may unduly restrict the utility 
12 
of the product or unnecessarily increase its cost because Interconnection Customers and 
13 
Transmission Owners would be denied the flexibility to utilize adjacent bays at the 
14 
substation for the generation and load lead lines when this is more practical or cost-
15 
effective than expanding the single bay that constitutes the Point of Interconnection to 
16 
accommodate both the load and generation lead lines.  The proposed language affords a 
17 
modicum of flexibility while still maintaining clear and narrow limits.  
18 
After considering stakeholder feedback and precedent on generator replacement, 
19 
MISO determined that allowing the load to connect at the same voltage level of the same 
20 
substation as the generation would be electrically indistinguishable from requiring them to 
21 
connect behind the same Point of Interconnection and that with the appropriate equipment, 
22 
injection to the rest of the Transmission System could be effectively limited in both 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 13 
 
 
scenarios.  Based on these considerations and stakeholder opposition to allowing ZG 
1 
Interconnection Service to address broader proximate load and generation configurations, 
2 
MISO determined that the proposed scope struck the best balance for the MISO footprint 
3 
between enabling large loads and protecting the Transmission System from broader 
4 
impacts.  
5 
 
 
MISO will continue to work with stakeholders on developing rules tailored to the 
6 
more dispersed proximate load and generation scenarios contemplated by the Show Cause 
7 
Order.  However, these solutions will be addressed in a separate Federal Power Act Section 
8 
205 Filing.  The current filing does not impede that separate effort.  
9 
Q. 
WHY DOES MISO PROPOSE ZG INTERCONNECTION SERVICE AS A 
10 
PERMANENT PRODUCT? 
11 
A. 
MISO proposes ZG Interconnection Service as a permanent product because the service is 
12 
designed for co-location arrangements in which generation is electrically tied to a specific 
13 
load at the same substation and voltage level and can be prevented from injecting into the 
14 
broader Transmission System.  A temporary service would create unnecessary costs and 
15 
uncertainty for generation and load in such configurations.  There are several reasons for 
16 
this determination.  First, allowing a permanent service will provide greater up-front 
17 
financial and operational certainty to the Interconnection Customer seeking ZG 
18 
Interconnection Service.  Second, as I testified earlier, ERIS is a broader product than is 
19 
needed to enable these types of arrangements.  If MISO were to make ZG Interconnection 
20 
Service temporary, this would result in the ZG Interconnection Customer that intends to 
21 
only continue to serve its co-located Load, later needing to pay unknown costs to go back 
22 
through the queue to obtain a service that it does not need and will not use.  Third, the 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 14 
 
 
limitations on injections to the rest of the Transmission System mitigate concerns about 
1 
impacts over time from the ZG Resource with ZG Interconnection Service because the 
2 
limitations on its injection are a core component of the product.  Should an Interconnection 
3 
Customer seek to change its configuration to allow broader injections, this would require 
4 
a new Interconnection Request for an appropriate service, such as ERIS or NRIS.  Fourth, 
5 
it would not be efficient or fair to weigh down the DPP with Interconnection Requests that 
6 
restudy generation and load that do not need to change their previously-studied 
7 
configuration because a time limit was placed on the original service type.  MISO 
8 
determined that the better limitation is the prohibition on injection.  If an Interconnection 
9 
Customer with ZG Interconnection Service seeks to serve different load or remove the 
10 
limitations included in ZG Interconnection Service, it may seek ERIS or NRIS service 
11 
through an appropriate Interconnection Request.  Barring such a change, the value of 
12 
having a durable service-when coupled with the limited configuration options that ZG 
13 
Interconnection Service authorizes—provides more value to the MISO footprint than 
14 
scoping ZG Interconnection Service as a temporary but electrically broader product. The 
15 
appropriate limiting feature for ZG Interconnection Service is the prohibition on injection 
16 
to the Transmission System, not an arbitrary time expiration. Given that ZG 
17 
Interconnection Service is continuously bounded by a narrow set of configurations and 
18 
operational options and is studied to ensure it does not affect the broader Transmission 
19 
System, a permanent service strikes the appropriate balance between reliability and 
20 
administrative efficiency.   
21 
 
 
To be clear, I am not stating that a temporary service is inappropriate for more 
22 
dispersed resource and load pairs—such as those that resemble the “proximate” 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 15 
 
 
configurations that the Commission describes in the Show Cause Order.  In fact, MISO 
1 
currently is exploring processes that accommodate such broader configurations with 
2 
stakeholders. 
3 
Q. 
CAN INTERCONNECTION CUSTOMERS COMBINE ZG INTERCONNECTION 
4 
SERVICE WITH OTHER INTERCONNECTION SERVICE TYPES? 
5 
A. 
No.  ZG Interconnection Service is fundamentally different from ERIS or NRIS service. 
6 
ZG Interconnection Service enables interconnection but excludes injections beyond the 
7 
substation where the ZG Resource and ZG Associated Load are interconnected. (except for 
8 
certain inevitable transient injection scenarios that I discuss below), while ERIS allows 
9 
injections of a specified amount as available, and NRIS allows unrestricted injections of a 
10 
specified amount.  ZG Interconnection Service and the ZGIA require configurations and/or 
11 
control technology to restrict injections onto the broader Transmission System.  
12 
Fundamentally, a resource cannot be interconnected with a prohibition on injection and 
13 
also have the right to inject onto the Transmission System.  For this reason, no amount of 
14 
ERIS or NRIS can be held by a Resource  at the same time that it has ZG Interconnection 
15 
Service. 
16 
Q. 
CAN AN INTERCONNECTION CUSTOMER WITH ZG INTERCONNECTION 
17 
SERVICE OBTAIN ERIS OR NRIS? 
18 
A. 
Yes.  An Interconnection Customer with ZG Interconnection Service is free to submit an 
19 
Interconnection Request into MISO’s queue for ERIS and/or NRIS.  Once the 
20 
Interconnection Customer completes studies and obtains ERIS or NRIS for its ZG 
21 
Resource, this automatically would supersede any ZG Interconnection Service that such 
22 
ZG Resource has and the parties would replace or amend the ZGIA with a GIA reflecting 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 16 
 
 
the new service levels.  This process applies, even where the Interconnection Customer 
1 
obtains a lesser megawatt amount of ERIS or NRIS than the ZG Interconnection Service it 
2 
previously had.  The reason for this is because the prohibition on injections and requirement 
3 
for equipment that electrically isolates the ZG Resource from the broader Transmission 
4 
System is being replaced with an ability to inject at some level. In such a circumstance, the 
5 
ZG Resource would then be treated as any other Generating Facility that has obtained 
6 
Interconnection Service below its installed capacity.  
7 
Q. 
PLEASE PROVIDE AN EXAMPLE OF THIS SCENARIO. 
8 
A. 
Assume a Generating Facility obtains ZG Interconnection Service for its full 500 MW of 
9 
installed capacity in order to serve a ZG Associated Load that is behind the Point of 
10 
Interconnection of the Generating Facility.  The Generating Facility would receive a 500 
11 
MW ZGIA and its appendices would describe the equipment necessary to limit injection 
12 
to the rest of the Transmission System.  Several years later, the Interconnection Customer 
13 
of this service decides that it wants to use same Generating Facility to serve loads elsewhere 
14 
on the Transmission System at certain times when the Demand associated with its co-
15 
located load may be reduced by 300 MW.  The Interconnection Customer would be able 
16 
to submit an Interconnection Request for 300 MW of ERIS or NRIS and proceed through 
17 
MISO’s queue (i.e., DPP) as would any other Interconnection Request.  At the conclusion 
18 
of the DPP, the Interconnection Customer would obtain a 300 MW GIA for ERIS or NRIS.  
19 
The appendices to such GIA would describe the Generating Facility, including its installed 
20 
capacity, as well as any metering or other equipment required under MISO’s ordinary 
21 
Tariff processes to facilitate such service below capacity.  This would replace the 
22 
requirement to maintain equipment that limits all injections beyond the substation 
23

Tab C 
 
 
 
Page 17

application was submitted.  The first ten projects to submit applications to be studied in

ZGIA will be tentatively selected until MISO has finalized its screening process of all ten

projects to ensure that they meet the ZGIA eligibility requirements.  After the ten projects

in a cycle are finalized, the remaining projects that applied in the cycle will be deferred to

the next available ZGIA cycle in order of submission time.  Since only ten projects will be

studied at a time, serial review of the applications will expedite the review process.  MISO

expects the ZGIA Interconnection Requests to apply when they are ready and meet all the

one exception. Since some jurisdictions allow resource ownership directly by the retail

entity that owns the ZG Associated Load that such entity is both permitted by applicable

law and intends to self-supply its ZG Associated Load through using onsite generation”.

for the next Operating Day.

Associated Load
